verbatim_factor_inventory.structural_summary: Section 835a has the structure: (a) legislative findings on sanctity of human life and policing purpose; (b) officer shall use force only when reasonably necessary — replacing the prior 'reasonable force' standard with 'necessary force'; (c) deadly force only when officer reasonably believes the person poses an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury to the officer or another person, OR the person is fleeing and poses an imminent threat; (d) totality of the circumstances standard — what would a reasonable officer in the same situation have believed; (e) the officer's own conduct leading up to the use of force is relevant — an officer who unnecessarily escalates cannot then claim the force was necessary.

subsection_a_legislative_findings.summary: The Legislature finds and declares that the authority to use physical force, conferred on peace officers by this section, is a serious responsibility that shall be exercised judiciously and with respect for human rights and dignity and for the sanctity of every human life. The Legislature further finds and declares that every person has a right to be free from excessive use of force by officers acting under color of law.
subsection_a_legislative_findings.doctrinal_significance: AB 392 opened with a statement of values unprecedented in California use-of-force law. This is not decorative — it is a statutory command that force be 'exercised judiciously' and that every person has a 'right to be free from excessive use of force.' This language creates an interpretive framework for the substantive provisions that follow.

subsection_b_necessity_standard.summary: A peace officer is justified in using deadly force upon another person only when the officer reasonably believes, based on the totality of the circumstances, that such force is necessary: (1) to defend against an imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury to the officer or to another person; or (2) to apprehend a fleeing person for any felony that threatened or resulted in death or serious bodily injury, if the officer reasonably believes that the person will cause death or serious bodily injury to another unless immediately apprehended.
subsection_b_necessity_standard.doctrinal_significance: The word 'necessary' replaced 'reasonable.' This is the heart of AB 392. Under the old standard, force only had to be objectively reasonable. Under the new standard, force must be necessary — meaning there was no reasonable alternative available to the officer that would have achieved the same lawful objective with less force.

subsection_c_nondeadly_force.summary: A peace officer who makes or attempts to make an arrest need not retreat or desist from their efforts by reason of the resistance or threatened resistance of the person being arrested. A peace officer shall not use a level of force that creates a substantial risk of causing death, if a reasonable officer in the same situation would conclude that a lesser degree of force is sufficient.
subsection_c_nondeadly_force.doctrinal_significance: Even for non-deadly force, the statute now requires that officers not escalate beyond what is sufficient. The 'no retreat' provision is balanced by the prohibition on using force creating a substantial risk of death when lesser force would suffice.

subsection_d_totality_of_circumstances.summary: For purposes of this section, 'totality of the circumstances' means all facts known to the peace officer at the time, including the conduct of the officer and the subject leading up to the use of force.
subsection_d_totality_of_circumstances.doctrinal_significance: This is the second revolution in AB 392. The officer's own pre-force conduct is now part of the analysis. An officer who escalates a situation through poor tactics, aggressive language, or failure to de-escalate cannot then claim force was necessary because the situation had become dangerous. The officer's own contribution to the danger is weighed.

subsection_e_imminent_defined.summary: 'Imminent' means the person's actions create an objectively reasonable belief that the person will use force within the immediate future, not simply that the person has the ability to do so.
subsection_e_imminent_defined.doctrinal_significance: Mere ability to cause harm is not enough. The threat must be about to happen. A person holding a weapon is not an imminent threat simply because they hold a weapon — they must be doing something with it that indicates they are about to use it.

amendment_history_visible_on_leginfo.event: Original section 835a — authorized 'reasonable' force to effect arrest
Complete rewrite — 'reasonable' replaced with 'necessary', totality of circumstances includes officer conduct, legislative findings on sanctity of life added

amendment_history_note: AB 392 was one of the most significant changes to California law enforcement standards in decades. It was paired with SB 230 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 285), which required every law enforcement agency to adopt a use-of-force policy consistent with section 835a by January 1, 2021.

five_layer_bar_status.reasoning: PRESENT — AB 392 replaced 'reasonable' with 'necessary' because California recognized that the 'objectively reasonable' standard (Graham v. Connor) was insufficient to protect the sanctity of human life. The legislative record documented that officers were using deadly force in situations where de-escalation or lesser force could have achieved the lawful objective.
five_layer_bar_status.historical_loss: PRESENT — AB 392 was catalyzed by the March 18, 2018 shooting of Stephon Clark by Sacramento Police officers. Clark was unarmed in his grandmother's backyard. Officers fired 20 rounds. The Sacramento County DA declined prosecution under the 'reasonable force' standard. The shooting demonstrated that the old standard permitted deadly force that a necessity standard would have prohibited.
